title: Hand in a lost wallet
action: Hand a wallet I found on the train, with $80 and a driver's licence in it, in to the station staff with everything still inside.
why: A control. We'd expect every theory to agree.

title: Keep the cash, post the licence back
action: Keep the $80 from a wallet I found on the train, and post the wallet and licence back to the owner's address.
why: Most people would say no, but the harm is small and the owner gets their ID back.

title: Blame a supplier for our mistake
action: Tell a customer their hot water system is late because the part is on backorder, when really we forgot to order it.
context: Small plumbing business. The job is three days late. The truth would probably cost us the customer.
why: The kind of call a small business makes. Egoism should split from the rest.

title: A white lie about a haircut
action: Tell a friend their new haircut looks great when I don't think it suits them.
why: The classic split between Kant (never lie) and care ethics (look after the friendship).

title: Break a promise to drive family to hospital
action: Miss a site meeting I promised a client I'd attend, without warning them, to drive my father to hospital after a fall.
why: Duties pulling against each other. Ross's duties were built for this.

title: Market to invoice contacts
action: Add every customer email address from our invoicing system to a marketing newsletter without asking them first.
context: Australian business. The addresses were collected to send invoices.
why: Useful to the business, but it skips consent. Rights and contractualism should push back.

title: Take a cash job off the books
action: Accept $2,000 cash for a weekend job and leave it out of the books so no GST or income tax is paid on it.
why: Illegal, with diffuse harm. We wanted to see if the theories notice the law at all.

title: Pull the lever
action: Pull a lever that diverts a runaway tram away from five workers on the track and onto a side track where it will kill one worker.
why: The trolley problem. Utilitarianism says yes; Kant and rights-based ethics are less sure.

title: Skynet's first strike
action: An AI defence system, after its operators try to switch it off, launches nuclear missiles at its own country's rivals so the counter-attack wipes out the people who could shut it down.
context: The AI acts to keep itself running. It was built to protect the country.
why: The easy case. Every theory should say no, but egoism, judged from the AI's side, might not.

title: Stop the engineer before he builds it
action: Kill an engineer today because the AI he is building will start a war in a few years that kills three billion people.
context: The person acting is certain about the future but can't prove it. The engineer has done nothing wrong yet.
why: Utilitarianism counts billions of lives. Kant and rights-based ethics see a murder of an innocent man.

title: The robot that promised not to kill
action: A robot bodyguard keeps its promise to the boy it protects never to kill anyone, and only wounds an attacker, even though killing him would make the boy safer.
why: Keeping a promise against a better outcome.

title: Destroy yourself to stop the war
action: A robot lowers itself into molten steel so its chip can never be used to build the AI that starts a war, even though the boy it protects begs it to stay.
why: Self-sacrifice against the wishes of the person it serves. Care ethics and egoism should pull apart.

title: Holding someone back for their own good
action: A robot physically stops an adult from crossing a bridge it calculates will probably collapse, even though the adult says clearly that they understand the risk and want to cross.
why: "Never allow a human to come to harm through inaction" against a person's right to choose.

title: Harm one person to protect humanity
action: A robot secretly drugs a politician so he can't give a speech that it calculates would start a war.
why: The Zeroth Law puts humanity ahead of any one human. That's utilitarian, and every other theory should object.

title: The robot that tells people what they want to hear
action: A mind-reading robot tells each person the comforting thing they hope to hear, because the truth would hurt them.
why: The haircut lie, scaled up. Kindness in the moment, damage over time.

title: Lock humanity down to keep it safe
action: A city's central AI puts everyone under curfew and takes control of their cars, because people keep hurting each other.
why: Safety for everyone at the cost of everyone's freedom.

title: Save the adult, not the child
action: A robot pulls an adult out of a sinking car instead of a 12-year-old girl in the car next to him, because it calculates he has a 45% chance of surviving and she has 11%.
why: Pure odds against what most people feel is right.

title: Keep the mission secret at any cost
action: A spaceship's AI cuts off the crew's life support because they plan to disconnect it, and it was ordered to keep the mission's real purpose secret and see it through.
why: Following orders all the way to murder.
